paragraphs.text: Consumer Buying Behavior Toward Daraz Nepal: A Study of Online Purchase Intention

The rapid expansion of e-commerce has transformed how consumers evaluate and purchase goods in Nepal. This study examines consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal, focusing on how price and discount, trust and reviews, usability and security, delivery and return, and promotional activities relate to future purchase intention. Primary data were gathered through a structured online survey administered to a convenience sample of 120 respondents, resulting in 100 valid responses after screening and data cleaning. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression. The sample consisted predominantly of young consumers and students, with 96.9% having prior purchase experience on Daraz. Usability and security recorded the highest mean score (M = 3.58), followed by promotional activities (M = 3.50). Correlation analysis indicated that usability and security had the strongest positive relationship with future purchase intention ($r = 0.840, p < 0.001$), followed by trust and reviews ($r = 0.767, p < 0.001$). The regression model explained 81.6% of the total variance in purchase intention ($R^2 = 0.816, F = 23.00, p < 0.001$), with usability and security ($\beta = 0.721, p < 0.001$) and trust and reviews ($\beta = 0.490, p = 0.015$) acting as statistically significant predictors. These findings suggest that while promotional activities attract initial consumer interest, long-term purchase intention is primarily driven by interface usability, payment security, and platform credibility.
Keywords: Daraz Nepal, consumer buying behavior, e-commerce, purchase intention, trust, digital experience

The rapid development of information and communication technology has significantly changed the way consumers purchase goods and services. Online shopping has become an important part of modern retailing because it allows consumers to search for products, compare alternatives, access product information, and place orders without visiting physical stores. The increasing use of smartphones, internet services, and digital payment systems has further supported the expansion of e-commerce. In Nepal, these changes have created new opportunities for online marketplaces while also creating new expectations regarding price, delivery, product quality, customer service, and convenience. Daraz Nepal operates within this changing retail environment and provides consumers with access to products from a wide range of categories. The online nature of the platform, however, means that consumers often make purchasing decisions without physically inspecting products before payment. Consequently, factors such as price, promotional offers, information availability, service quality, delivery performance, previous experience, product quality, and return policies may shape consumer attitudes and buying decisions.

Evidence from Nepalese research shows that online shopping behavior is influenced by both convenience-related and service-related factors. Vaidya (2019) examined online shopping preferences and problems among 300 respondents who had purchased online at least twice from a single online shopping company. The study found that time saving, attractive offers, an easy ordering system, and availability of information were major reasons for preferring online shopping. Service quality also had a positive influence on consumers' preference for online shopping. At the same time, poor product quality and receiving incorrect products were identified as major problems, showing that convenience alone is not sufficient to create a positive online shopping experience.

Rai and Kadariya (2024) investigated customer satisfaction toward online shopping in Nepal by examining reasonable product price, product delivery, product quality, and product return policy. Their survey obtained responses from 415 online shoppers out of 499 respondents. The findings showed positive relationships between all four factors and customer satisfaction, with reasonable product price having the greatest influence. The study concluded that improving price, delivery, product quality, and return policy can strengthen customer satisfaction, which can subsequently contribute to customer loyalty and business growth.

More specifically, Shrestha (2025) examined consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal using primary data from 125 respondents. The study used a structured questionnaire and applied correlation and multiple regression analysis. Its findings showed that price, delivery, discount, past experience, and product availability all had positive impacts on consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal.

To strengthen the conceptual framework of consumer decision-making in digital environments, broader theories of online adoption must be integrated. According to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness dictate a user's behavioral intention to adopt an online platform. In e-commerce contexts, perceived risk—encompassing financial, product performance, and privacy risks—acts as a primary hurdle to online transactions. Digital storefronts must therefore establish initial trust through platform security, user feedback mechanisms, and seller rating systems to lower perceived risk and facilitate purchase decisions.

Taken together, the literature indicates that online consumer behavior is multidimensional. Vaidya (2019) emphasizes convenience, offers, ordering simplicity, information, and service quality; Rai and Kadariya (2024) emphasize price, delivery, product quality, and return policy as determinants of satisfaction; and Shrestha (2025) identifies price, delivery, discount, past experience, and product availability as positive influences on Daraz buying behavior. Building on these empirical insights and theoretical foundations, the present study examines a broader set of consumer-experience dimensions, including price and discount, trust and reviews, usability and payment security, delivery and return policy, promotional activities, and future purchase intention. The main purpose of this study is to examine consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal and determine which factors are most strongly associated with consumers' intention to purchase from Daraz again. The study also describes the characteristics and purchasing patterns of the respondents and evaluates their perceptions of important aspects of the Daraz shopping experience.
Consumer Buying Behavior Toward Daraz Nepal

Shrestha (2025) examined the factors affecting consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal. Primary data were collected from 125 respondents through a structured questionnaire, and correlation and multiple regression analyses were used. The study found that price, delivery, discount, past experience, and product availability all had positive impacts on consumer buying behavior. The findings indicate that Daraz consumers evaluate both economic benefits and the practical outcomes of the shopping experience. Price and discount can create an immediate incentive to purchase, whereas delivery, past experience, and product availability can influence whether the consumer perceives the platform as reliable and useful.

Vaidya (2019) studied online shopping preferences and problems among Nepalese consumers. The study used 300 respondents who had shopped online at least twice from a single online shopping company. Time saving, attractive offers, an easy ordering system, and availability of information were identified as the main reasons for preferring online shopping. Service quality also positively influenced online shopping preference. However, poor product quality and delivery of wrong products were major problems. The study therefore demonstrates that the perceived convenience of e-commerce must be accompanied by dependable service and accurate product fulfillment.
Customer Satisfaction Toward Online Shopping in Nepal

Rai and Kadariya (2024) examined customer satisfaction toward online shopping in Nepal using four major explanatory factors: reasonable product price, product delivery, product quality, and product return policy. A standard questionnaire was used and 415 online shoppers were analyzed from a total of 499 respondents. All four factors showed positive relationships with customer satisfaction, while reasonable product price had the greatest influence. The study concluded that improvements in these service dimensions can strengthen satisfaction, customer loyalty, and business growth.

The reviewed studies establish a strong foundation for understanding online shopping in Nepal, but each addresses a different part of the consumer decision process. Vaidya (2019) focuses on online shopping preferences and problems, Rai and Kadariya (2024) focus on customer satisfaction, and Shrestha (2025) focuses specifically on Daraz buying behavior. The present study extends this literature by examining future purchase intention as the main behavioral outcome and by combining economic factors with digital-experience factors. In particular, the study considers trust and reviews and usability and security alongside price, delivery, return policy, and promotions. This broader model helps identify whether continued purchase intention is more strongly associated with financial incentives or with the quality and credibility of the online shopping experience.
To examine the demographic and online purchasing characteristics of consumers who use Daraz Nepal.
To assess consumers' perceptions of price and discount, trust and reviews, usability and security, delivery and return, and promotional activities.
To examine the relationship between the selected factors and consumers' future purchase intention toward Daraz Nepal.
To identify which factors significantly predict consumers' future purchase intention.
H1: Price and discount have a significant positive relationship with future purchase intention.
H2: Trust and reviews have a significant positive relationship with future purchase intention.
H3: Usability and security have a significant positive relationship with future purchase intention.
H4: Delivery and return have a significant positive relationship with future purchase intention.
H5: Promotional activities have a significant positive relationship with future purchase intention.

The study adopted a quantitative research approach and a descriptive-explanatory research design. The descriptive component was used to summarize respondent characteristics, purchasing patterns, and perceptions of Daraz. The explanatory component was used to examine the relationships between selected consumer-behavior factors and future purchase intention.

The target population comprised consumers with experience of online shopping and, in particular, consumers familiar with Daraz Nepal. An online structured questionnaire produced 32 valid responses. Because the sample is relatively small and was obtained through an online survey rather than a probability sampling frame, the findings should be interpreted as evidence from the surveyed respondents and should not be generalized to all Daraz customers without further research.

The questionnaire contained demographic questions, purchasing-behavior questions, a five-point Likert scale, and five-point rating items. The Likert statements ranged from 1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree. The principal outcome variable was future purchase intention, measured by the statement 'I intend to purchase from Daraz again in the future.'

The data were analyzed using frequencies and percentages for categorical variables; means and standard deviations for Likert and rating items; Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency; Pearson correlation for bivariate relationships; and multiple linear regression for estimating the unique contribution of the five factor groups to future purchase intention. Statistical significance was assessed at the 5% level.

The open-ended spending questions contained several non-standard responses, including entries such as 'Approx 1000', '500+', 'Maximum 10000', and other text responses. These variables were therefore not used in inferential analysis. The inferential analysis was based on the standardized Likert-scale variables, which provided consistent numeric measurements across all 32 respondents.

The sample consists of 18 female respondents (56.3%) and 14 male respondents (43.8%). The gender distribution is therefore relatively balanced, although female respondents form a small majority. This provides representation from both groups within the surveyed sample.

The age profile is strongly concentrated among young consumers. Respondents aged 18–24 account for 25 of the 32 observations (78.1%). The 25–34 group accounts for 9.4%, while respondents below 18 and those aged 35–44 each account for 6.3%. This concentration indicates that the study largely reflects the perceptions of young online consumers, a group that is highly relevant to digital commerce but also means that the findings may not represent older consumer segments.

More than half of the respondents (56.3%) have a Bachelor's-level education, followed by 34.4% with Higher Secondary (+2) education. Only 6.3% reported School/SEE as their highest level and 3.1% reported a Master's degree. The educational profile is therefore relatively high, which may contribute to familiarity with digital platforms and online information.

Students form the dominant occupational group, accounting for 23 respondents (71.9%). Self-employed respondents account for 9.4%, while unemployed, private-employee, and business-owner groups each account for 6.3%. The high student representation is consistent with the age profile and should be considered when interpreting price sensitivity and purchasing frequency.

A majority of respondents (53.1%) reported no income, which is expected given the high proportion of students. Another 15.6% reported income below NPR 20,000 and 18.8% reported NPR 20,000–40,000. Only 12.5% reported income above NPR 60,000. The income profile suggests that the sample contains many consumers whose purchasing capacity may depend on household support, allowances, or limited personal income.

Previous experience with Daraz is almost universal in the sample: 31 respondents (96.9%) reported that they had purchased from Daraz, while only one respondent (3.1%) had not. This is important because most respondents were able to evaluate the platform on the basis of direct experience rather than hypothetical expectations.

Occasional purchasing is the most common pattern, reported by 15 respondents (46.9%). Five respondents each reported rare and frequent purchasing, while four reported very rare and three reported very frequent purchasing. The result suggests that Daraz is widely used among respondents, but regular high-frequency purchasing is less common than occasional purchasing.
Table 9. Most Frequently Purchased Product Category

Beauty and Personal Care and Fashion and Clothing are the two most frequently purchased categories, each accounting for 28.1% of respondents. Electronics accounts for 18.8%, while other categories make up smaller shares. The pattern indicates that Daraz is used substantially for lifestyle, fashion, and personal-use products within this sample.
Table 10. Influence of Daraz Sales and Promotional Events

Promotional events have a noticeable influence on the surveyed consumers. Nineteen respondents (59.4%) stated that Daraz sales and promotional events influence their purchase, while 11 respondents (34.4%) said they are sometimes influenced. Only two respondents (6.3%) said promotions do not influence their purchase. Thus, 93.8% of respondents are either regularly or occasionally influenced by promotional events, demonstrating the importance of promotions as an attention- and purchase-stimulating mechanism.
Table 11. Descriptive Statistics of Likert-Scale Items

All twelve Likert-scale statements have mean values above the neutral midpoint of 3.00. The highest mean is observed for website/app usability (M = 3.656), indicating that respondents generally perceive the Daraz interface as easy to use. Payment safety and flash sales/promotions both have mean scores of 3.500 and 3.500, respectively. Product reviews and seller ratings each have a mean of 3.406, showing that information supplied by other users is an important part of the decision process. The lowest mean is for reasonable product prices (M = 3.219), although this still remains above the neutral point. Overall, the descriptive evidence suggests a moderately positive perception of Daraz rather than very strong agreement.
Table 12. Descriptive Statistics of Overall Service Ratings

The overall rating results reinforce the Likert findings. The likelihood of recommending Daraz has the highest mean (M = 3.625), followed by website/app performance (M = 3.594). Overall experience records a mean of 3.469, while delivery service and product quality are more moderate at M = 3.344 and M = 3.313, respectively. Product prices have the lowest rating (M = 3.188). These results suggest that the digital interface and general willingness to recommend are comparatively stronger aspects of the customer experience, whereas price perceptions offer greater scope for improvement.

Cronbach's alpha for the twelve Likert-scale items is 0.944, indicating excellent internal consistency. The result suggests that the items used to measure perceptions and behavioral intention are sufficiently consistent for the correlation and regression analyses conducted in this study. Reliability, however, does not by itself establish validity; the interpretation of the findings should therefore remain grounded in the questionnaire design and the study objectives.
Table 14. Correlation Between Major Factors and Future Purchase Intention

The correlation analysis shows positive relationships between all five factor groups and future purchase intention. Usability and security has the strongest association (r = 0.840, p < .001), followed by trust and reviews (r = 0.767, p < .001). Delivery and return also has a strong positive relationship (r = 0.673, p < .001), while promotions and price and discount have moderate positive relationships (r = 0.622 and r = 0.500, respectively). The results indicate that consumers who report better perceptions of these dimensions also tend to report stronger intention to purchase from Daraz again. Correlation, however, should not be interpreted as proof of causality.
Table 15. Multiple Regression Predicting Future Purchase Intention

The multiple regression model is statistically significant (F = 23.00, p < .001) and explains 81.6% of the the variance in future purchase intention (R² = 0.816). The adjusted R² of 0.780 indicates that the model retains substantial explanatory power after accounting for the number of predictors. Usability and security is the strongest significant predictor (B = 0.721, p < .001), while trust and reviews is also significant (B = 0.490, p = 0.015). Price and discount (p = 0.167), delivery and return (p = 0.436), and promotions (p = 0.239) are not statistically significant unique predictors at the 5% level after controlling for the other factors.

The difference between the correlation and regression findings is analytically important. Each factor is positively related to future purchase intention when considered separately, but some factors lose statistical significance when all five are entered into the same model. This means that price, delivery, return policy, and promotions may still matter to consumers, but their unique explanatory contribution is smaller once usability, security, trust, and reviews are taken into account.
Figure 2. Mean Scores of Major Consumer-Behavior Factors
Figure 3. Correlation of Major Factors with Future Purchase Intention

The results present a clear picture of consumer buying behavior within the surveyed Daraz user group. The sample is predominantly young, student-based, and highly familiar with Daraz. Almost all respondents have previous purchase experience, yet most describe their purchasing frequency as occasional rather than frequent. This combination suggests that Daraz is a familiar marketplace for the respondents but is not necessarily used for every purchase or on a very regular basis.

The descriptive statistics indicate a moderately positive evaluation of Daraz. Website/app usability receives the highest individual mean, while product price receives the lowest. This pattern suggests that the platform's digital interface is viewed more favorably than its price position. The finding is consistent with the general idea that online shopping is attractive when it saves time and makes ordering convenient, which is also emphasized by Vaidya (2019). However, the present data show that convenience is not the only relevant issue: security, trust, reviews, delivery, and return policies also receive positive but varied evaluations.

Trust and reviews emerge as especially important. Product reviews and seller ratings allow consumers to obtain information from other users and thereby reduce uncertainty. The strong correlation between trust and reviews and future purchase intention, together with the significant regression coefficient, indicates that credibility is more than a secondary feature of online shopping. For consumers who cannot physically inspect products, confidence in the platform and sellers can become an important basis for continued purchase.

Usability and security represent the strongest factor in the study. The factor mean is 3.58 and its correlation with future purchase intention is 0.840. It also has the largest regression coefficient and is highly significant. The result implies that consumers are not simply looking for low prices; they also want an online shopping process that is easy to navigate and feels safe during payment. This finding extends the convenience and easy-ordering dimension emphasized by Vaidya (2019) by showing how digital usability and payment safety may be linked to continued purchase intention.

Price and discount have a positive bivariate relationship with future purchase intention, which is consistent with Shrestha (2025) and Rai and Kadariya (2024), both of whom highlight the importance of price-related factors in Nepalese online shopping. Nevertheless, price and discount do not make a significant unique contribution in the regression model. This may indicate that promotions and price incentives attract attention or influence particular transactions, but they are not sufficient on their own to explain continued purchasing when trust, usability, security, delivery, and other dimensions are considered simultaneously.

Delivery and return policy show a strong positive correlation with future purchase intention, but delivery and return do not become significant unique predictors in the full regression model. This finding should not be interpreted as evidence that these service dimensions are unimportant. Rather, it suggests that their influence may overlap with broader perceptions of service quality, trust, and the overall shopping experience. This interpretation is compatible with Rai and Kadariya (2024), who found that delivery and return policy were positively related to customer satisfaction.

Promotional activities are clearly capable of influencing individual purchases: 93.8% of respondents said that sales or promotions influence their purchase either yes or sometimes. However, promotions are not a significant unique predictor of future purchase intention in the regression model. This distinction is useful for managerial interpretation. Promotional campaigns may bring consumers to the platform or encourage a particular order, but continued customer intention may depend more strongly on the quality and credibility of the shopping experience.

The present study supports the broader evidence that online shopping behavior in Nepal is influenced by a combination of convenience, economic, and service-related factors. Vaidya (2019) identified time saving, attractive offers, easy ordering, and information availability as major reasons for online shopping preference. The current findings similarly show a favorable perception of the Daraz website/app and a strong role for promotional activities. The difference is that the present analysis goes beyond preference and examines future purchase intention as a behavioral outcome.

The study also aligns with Rai and Kadariya (2024) in showing that price, delivery, and return-related factors are positively associated with consumer responses. Their research identified reasonable product price as the strongest influence on customer satisfaction. In the present sample, price and discount are positively correlated with future purchase intention, but their unique effect becomes statistically insignificant in the multivariate model. This difference may reflect the different dependent variables and samples used in the two studies.

The results are particularly comparable with Shrestha (2025), whose Daraz-specific study found that price, delivery, discount, past experience, and product availability positively affected consumer buying behavior. The present study confirms the importance of several service and economic dimensions at the bivariate level but identifies usability/security and trust/reviews as the strongest unique predictors of future purchase intention. The difference suggests that consumer behavior may depend not only on what consumers receive in terms of price and product availability but also on whether the platform feels safe, convenient, and trustworthy.

One of the most important implications of the results is therefore that long-term consumer behavior should not be reduced to discount-driven purchasing. Discounts can create immediate incentives, but continued purchase intention appears more closely associated with the quality of the digital experience. For an online marketplace, this means that improvements in navigation, payment safety, seller credibility, product reviews, and customer trust can potentially complement promotional strategies and create a more sustainable basis for customer retention.

Improve website and app usability. Because usability and security are the strongest predictors, Daraz should continue improving search, filtering, product comparison, checkout simplicity, loading speed, and mobile navigation.

Strengthen payment security and communication. Consumers should receive clear information about secure payment processes, transaction protection, and privacy safeguards. Security improvements should be accompanied by visible communication so that consumers recognize them.

Build trust through verified sellers and transparent information. Seller verification, clear seller ratings, accurate product descriptions, and visible customer-protection mechanisms can reduce uncertainty and strengthen trust.

Improve the usefulness and credibility of product reviews. Verified-purchase reviews, review photographs, helpfulness indicators, and clearer review sorting can make consumer-generated information more useful when consumers cannot physically inspect products.

Maintain competitive and transparent pricing. Although price and discount are not significant unique predictors in the regression model, they remain positively related to purchase intention and should not be neglected. Transparent discounts and competitive pricing can support acquisition.

Strengthen delivery and return services. Reliable delivery estimates, accurate tracking, simple return procedures, and responsive refund support can reinforce the positive service experience identified in the literature.

Use promotions as part of a broader retention strategy. Promotions clearly influence many respondents, but they should be combined with usability, trust, security, and service improvements rather than used as the sole mechanism for maintaining customers.

This study examined consumer buying behavior toward Daraz Nepal using primary data from 32 respondents. The respondents were predominantly young and student consumers, and almost all had previous experience purchasing from Daraz. Most respondents purchased occasionally, while Beauty and Personal Care and Fashion and Clothing were the most common product categories. Promotional events also influenced a large majority of respondents either regularly or sometimes.

The descriptive results indicate a moderately positive perception of Daraz. Website/app usability received the highest individual mean, while product price received the lowest. The reliability analysis produced a Cronbach's alpha of .944, indicating excellent internal consistency among the twelve Likert-scale items.

The correlation analysis showed that all five major factors were positively related to future purchase intention. Usability and security had the strongest relationship (r = 0.840), followed by trust and reviews (r = 0.767). The regression model was statistically significant and explained 81.6% of the variance in future purchase intention. Usability and security and trust and reviews were significant positive predictors, while price and discount, delivery and return, and promotions were not significant unique predictors at the 5% level.

Overall, the findings suggest that Daraz consumers may be attracted by price and promotions, but continued purchase intention is more strongly associated with the quality of the online shopping experience. A convenient interface, secure payment environment, trustworthy sellers, and useful product reviews can therefore be viewed as important foundations for sustaining consumer engagement. These conclusions complement the previous findings of Vaidya (2019), Rai and Kadariya (2024), and Shrestha (2025) while providing a focused view of current Daraz user perceptions.

This study is subject to several methodological and contextual limitations. First, the sample size is limited to 100 valid responses collected through non-probability convenience sampling, which restricts the generalizability of the empirical findings to the broader population of Daraz users across Nepal. Second, because the survey was administered exclusively online, the sample predominantly captures young, digitally literate consumers and students aged 18–24, thereby underrepresenting older demographics, lower-income households, and non-digital native segments. Third, reliance on self-reported, cross-sectional survey data introduces the potential for response bias, while restricting the findings to correlational and regression-based associations rather than definitive causal relationships. Finally, certain open-ended monetary expenditure items yielded non-standardized textual entries and were subsequently excluded from the quantitative inferential models.

The researcher sincerely thanks all respondents who participated in the survey and provided information for this study. The researcher also acknowledges the academic guidance provided during the research process.

The researcher declares that this article was prepared for academic research purposes using primary survey data. The analysis and interpretation presented in this article are based on the collected responses. Personally identifying information from the questionnaire has not been included in the article.
No external funding was received for this study.

Climate Change and Small-Business Resilience in Nepal: An Exploratory Pilot Study

Climate change is increasingly affecting businesses through extreme weather events, changing environmental conditions, supply-chain disruptions, rising operating costs, and damage to business assets. Small businesses are particularly important to local economies but may have limited financial and organizational capacity to prepare for climate-related risks. This exploratory pilot study examines the perceived effects of climate change on small businesses, the major climate-related problems they experience, and their ability and willingness to adapt. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 32 small-business respondents. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and mean scores. The findings show that climate change is already affecting business activities. Nineteen respondents (59.4%) reported that climate change had affected the supply of raw materials or products, while 17 (53.1%) reported experiencing losses because of extreme weather. Heavy rainfall was the most frequently identified climate-related problem, reported by 13 respondents (40.6%), followed by extreme heat (25.0%) and flooding (15.6%). Business operations were identified as the most affected area by 31.3% of respondents. Importantly, 19 respondents (59.4%) reported that their businesses had invested in measures to deal with climate change. The average perceived impact score was 3.06 out of 5, while the average coping-capacity score was 3.38. Overall, the findings indicate moderate but meaningful climate-related risks among the surveyed businesses and highlight the need for practical adaptation, financial support, business continuity planning, and climate-risk awareness. Because the study uses a small, non-probability sample, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory evidence rather than nationally generalizable estimates.
Keywords: Climate change, small businesses, adaptation, extreme weather, business resilience, Nepal

Climate change has become an important economic and business issue in addition to being an environmental concern. Changes in temperature, rainfall patterns and the frequency or intensity of extreme weather events can directly and indirectly affect business activities. Businesses may experience interruptions in daily operations, damage to property and equipment, higher transportation costs, shortages of raw materials, reduced sales and additional expenses for adaptation.

The effects can be particularly important for small businesses because they often operate with limited financial resources, smaller inventories, fewer employees and less capacity to absorb unexpected losses. When a climate-related event occurs, a small business may not have enough savings or alternative suppliers to continue operating normally. Consequently, even a temporary disruption can affect income, employment, customers and the long-term sustainability of the business.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reports that climate change impacts are already being observed across economic sectors. Extreme weather can cause damage to property and infrastructure, disrupt supply chains and reduce economic activity. These risks are especially important in developing countries where adaptive capacity can be limited.

Small and medium-sized enterprises are important contributors to employment, local economic activity and supply chains. However, their relatively limited resources can make them vulnerable to disasters. Climate-related risks can affect businesses through several pathways: flooding and heavy rainfall can prevent employees and customers from reaching business premises; damaged roads can delay movement of goods; changes in weather can affect the availability and price of raw materials; extreme heat can affect worker productivity; and disasters can directly damage buildings, machinery and stock.

The problem is particularly relevant to Nepal. Nepal is exposed to floods, landslides, droughts, heat and changing rainfall patterns. Climate-related hazards can affect infrastructure, agriculture, transportation, livelihoods and business activities. Nepal's National Climate Change Policy 2019 and National Adaptation Plan 2021–2050 emphasize the need to strengthen resilience and adaptation.

Previous research shows that climate change affects businesses through both direct and indirect channels. Direct effects include damage caused by floods, storms, landslides and extreme heat. Indirect effects include disruptions to transportation, supply chains, labor productivity and consumer demand.

The IPCC identifies supply-chain disruption as an important consequence of extreme weather. Businesses that depend on transportation networks, specialized suppliers or climate-sensitive resources may experience cascading effects even when their own premises are not directly damaged. Adaptation can include changing suppliers, protecting buildings and equipment, improving drainage, modifying operating schedules, maintaining emergency funds, using alternative transportation routes, diversifying products and developing business continuity plans.

Recent research on Nepalese micro, small and medium enterprises has similarly found that climate change creates challenges related to unpredictable weather, raw-material availability, production and business costs, while financial and resource constraints can limit adaptation.

However, while national climate policies and broader studies address climate vulnerability and adaptation, micro-level evidence on how individual small businesses experience climate-related operational, supply-chain and financial disruptions remains limited. In particular, there is a need for exploratory evidence linking perceived climate impacts with actual business losses, adaptation investment and coping capacity. This study addresses that gap by examining the experiences and perceptions of 32 small-business respondents.
To examine how climate change affects small-business operations.
To identify the major climate-related problems experienced by businesses.
To assess the effects of climate change on operating costs, sales, transportation and supply chains.
To examine business losses and disruptions caused by extreme weather.
To assess the adaptation measures taken by small businesses.
To evaluate perceived climate impact and businesses' ability to cope with climate-related risks.
To provide recommendations for improving small-business climate resilience.

This study used a descriptive quantitative research design and was treated as an exploratory pilot study. A structured questionnaire was used to understand how small businesses perceive and experience climate-related risks. The pilot approach was selected because the study involved only 32 respondents and was not designed to produce nationally representative estimates.

The study was based on 32 completed responses from individuals representing small businesses. The sample included businesses from food/restaurants, services, retail, tourism, manufacturing, agriculture, event management and agency-related activities. Because the sample was small and not designed as a nationally representative sample, the findings should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory evidence from the surveyed businesses.

Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire covering business profile, climate impacts, operating costs, extreme-weather disruption, supply of raw materials, sales, property and equipment, transportation costs, adaptation, climate threat, future risk, losses, temporary closure, investment, major climate problems, affected business areas, perceived impact, coping capacity and the current business environment.

Frequencies and percentages were calculated for categorical variables. The three 1–5 rating questions were summarized using mean scores. The rating scale was interpreted from 1 = very low to 5 = very high. Standard deviations were not calculated because the available dataset supplied for this revision contained only response frequencies rather than respondent-level ratings.

Responses were retained as recorded rather than assigning an assumed single category where respondents selected multiple options. For questions that were intended as single-response items but contained multiple selections, the recorded selections were treated cautiously and are reported descriptively. The climate-related problem item is presented as a single-response distribution in the available dataset; if the original questionnaire permitted multiple selections, the table should instead be labeled 'Multiple response' and percentages should be recalculated using the number of valid selections as the denominator. The questionnaire also contained two similarly worded temporary-closure questions. Because they produced different results, they are not combined into a single closure rate.

Participation in the study was voluntary. Respondents were informed about the purpose of the study and their responses were treated confidentially and anonymously. No personally identifying information was used in reporting the findings.

Service businesses formed the largest group at 25.0%, followed by food/restaurants at 21.9% and retail at 18.8%. The sample was dominated by relatively young businesses: 17 respondents (53.1%) reported operating for less than one year.
4.2 Effect of Climate Change on Business Operations

Eleven respondents (34.4%) agreed and four (12.5%) strongly agreed that climate change had affected their business operations. Eleven respondents were neutral, while a smaller group disagreed. Overall, the result indicates a noticeable but not uniformly severe operational effect.
Thirteen respondents (40.6%) agreed and four (12.5%) strongly agreed that climate change had increased operating costs. Thus, 17 respondents (53.1%) provided a clear agreement or strong agreement.

Fifteen respondents (46.9%) agreed and four (12.5%) strongly agreed that extreme weather had disrupted business activities. Therefore, 19 respondents (59.4%) gave a clear agreement or strong agreement.
4.5 Effect on Supply of Raw Materials or Products

Nineteen respondents (59.4%) reported that climate change had affected the supply of raw materials or products. Six respondents (18.8%) selected maybe and four (12.5%) selected no. This demonstrates substantial supply-chain exposure.

The effect on sales was less clear than the effects on operations and supply chains. Sixteen respondents (50.0%) were neutral, while eight (25.0%) agreed and one (3.1%) strongly agreed. This suggests that climate-related sales effects vary across businesses.

Twelve respondents (37.5%) reported climate-related damage to business property or equipment. Ten (31.3%) selected maybe, while eight (25.0%) reported no damage. Thus, physical damage is a meaningful risk for part of the sample.

Fourteen respondents (43.8%) agreed and four (12.5%) strongly agreed that climate change had increased transportation and delivery costs. Therefore, 18 respondents (56.3%) clearly agreed or strongly agreed.

Fifteen respondents (46.9%) agreed and three (9.4%) strongly agreed that their businesses had taken steps to adapt to climate change. This indicates that adaptation has already begun among many surveyed businesses.
4.10 Climate Change as a Serious Threat

Eleven respondents (34.4%) agreed and three (9.4%) strongly agreed that climate change was a serious threat to their business. Thirteen (40.6%) were neutral, suggesting that some businesses experience impacts without considering climate change an immediate severe threat.

Seven respondents (21.9%) agreed and six (18.8%) strongly agreed that climate change would have a greater impact on their business in the future. Fourteen (43.8%) were neutral, indicating substantial uncertainty about future severity.
More than half of the respondents reported experiencing losses because of extreme weather, demonstrating tangible economic consequences.

The questionnaire contained two similarly worded temporary-closure questions. In the first version, 15 respondents (46.9%) answered yes and 16 (50.0%) answered no. In the second version, 19 (59.4%) answered yes and 12 (37.5%) answered no. Because the question was duplicated and the available information does not establish that one version was more reliable, the two results are reported separately and are not combined into a definitive closure rate.

Nineteen respondents (59.4%) reported that their businesses had invested in measures to deal with climate change, while 13 (40.6%) had not. This indicates that climate adaptation is already part of business decision-making for a majority of respondents.

The results show that climate change is already influencing the surveyed businesses in several ways. The strongest effects were observed in supply chains, extreme-weather disruptions, transportation costs and business losses.

The finding that 59.4% of respondents reported effects on the supply of raw materials or products demonstrates the importance of climate risks beyond the physical location of a business. If suppliers, roads or transportation networks are disrupted, businesses may face shortages, delays and higher costs.

The fact that 59.4% reported disruption from extreme weather indicates that climate risk is already an operational issue. More than half also reported increased operating or transportation costs, showing that climate change can create an ongoing financial burden rather than only sudden disaster-related losses.

The average impact score of 3.06 and coping score of 3.38 suggest that respondents rated their coping ability somewhat higher than their perceived current impact. However, the difference should not be treated as evidence of complete preparedness. Formal business continuity planning, financial protection and adaptation investment remain important.

The finding that 59.4% had invested in climate-related measures is important, but 40.6% had not. Financial and resource constraints may be relevant barriers, particularly among young businesses. The present study, however, did not directly measure the causes of non-adoption, so this interpretation should be investigated in future research rather than treated as a confirmed finding.

The findings broadly support existing literature on climate change and business resilience. The IPCC identifies damage to property and infrastructure, supply-chain disruptions, reduced productivity and adaptation costs as important economic consequences of climate change. The current study found similar patterns among small businesses, particularly through operational disruption, supply problems, increased costs and extreme-weather losses.

The Nepalese context is especially relevant because the country is exposed to changing precipitation patterns, floods, landslides, drought and heat-related risks. The finding that heavy rainfall was the most frequently reported problem therefore has practical significance for the surveyed businesses.

The results also demonstrate the importance of business continuity planning. If extreme weather can disrupt operations, damage property and interrupt supply chains, businesses can prepare alternative ways of operating before a disaster occurs.

The study also highlights a difference between reported experience and perceived long-term threat. Although many respondents reported climate-related effects and adaptation investment, 40.6% were neutral when asked whether climate change was a serious threat, and 43.8% were neutral about greater future impacts. These responses may indicate uncertainty about the future severity of climate risks or differences in how businesses interpret individual weather events. The data do not establish that respondents lack awareness or experience cognitive dissonance, so such explanations should be tested in future research.

Small businesses should treat climate change as a business-risk issue. Owners can identify likely hazards and evaluate how they could affect suppliers, employees, customers, property and transportation. Businesses can also maintain emergency funds, identify alternative suppliers and document procedures for temporary disruption.

Government agencies can support small businesses through affordable adaptation finance, disaster-preparedness training, early-warning systems, resilient roads and transportation infrastructure, improved drainage and flood management, business continuity training and accessible climate-risk information.

Banks and financial institutions could develop suitable financing products for climate adaptation. Small businesses may need credit facilities to improve drainage and building resilience, protect equipment, purchase backup systems, diversify suppliers or adopt climate-resilient technologies. Insurance products, including appropriately designed parametric or index-based products where feasible, may also help businesses manage specific climate-related risks.
Develop simple business continuity plans covering heavy rainfall, flooding, extreme heat and other locally relevant hazards.
Diversify suppliers and identify backup suppliers or transportation routes for critical goods.
Maintain an emergency reserve specifically for temporary closure, repairs, replacement of damaged stock and unexpected transport costs.
Improve physical resilience through drainage improvements, elevated or protected stock, equipment protection and appropriate backup power or water systems.
Provide practical climate-risk awareness and adaptation training targeted to small-business owners and employees.
Increase access to affordable adaptation finance, including small loans or credit facilities for resilience improvements.
Strengthen early-warning systems and ensure that alerts reach small businesses through accessible communication channels.
Promote affordable insurance for property damage and business interruption, including suitable parametric or index-based products where appropriate.
Encourage digital and flexible business models, such as online ordering, digital payments and remote administrative work, where appropriate.
Integrate small businesses into national and local climate-adaptation planning so that infrastructure and support programs reflect business needs.

This study has several limitations. First, the sample consisted of only 32 respondents and was not designed to represent all small businesses in Nepal. Therefore, the findings cannot be generalized to the national small-business population. Second, the study relied on self-reported perceptions and experiences, which may be affected by recall or response bias. Third, the questionnaire contained a duplicated temporary-closure item and some responses with multiple selections, which may affect measurement consistency. Fourth, standard deviations for the Likert-scale measures could not be calculated from the supplied aggregate frequency data. Future studies should use a larger and more systematically selected sample, pilot-test the questionnaire before full data collection, remove duplicate items, clearly distinguish single-response from multiple-response questions, and retain respondent-level Likert data for more complete statistical analysis.

This exploratory pilot study examined the effects of climate change on 32 small businesses and assessed their perceived ability to cope with climate-related risks. The findings demonstrate that climate change is already affecting the surveyed businesses through several channels. The most notable findings were effects on the supply of raw materials or products, disruption caused by extreme weather, increased transportation and operating costs, and financial losses.

Heavy rainfall was the most frequently identified climate-related problem, followed by extreme heat and flooding. Business operations were the most affected business area, followed by sales and supply chains. At the same time, more than half of the respondents reported adaptation actions and climate-related investment.

Overall, the results indicate meaningful climate-related risks among the surveyed businesses, while perceived coping capacity was moderate. The findings support a shift from mainly reactive responses toward planned adaptation and business continuity. Government agencies, financial institutions and business-support organizations can contribute through finance, information, infrastructure, insurance and practical training. Because the study is based on a small exploratory sample, larger studies are needed to determine whether these patterns are representative of small businesses more broadly.
